headline: Healey's first Budget offers £100 energy payment, taxes banks and brings forward defence target

terms.meaning: Self-imposed limits on how much the government can borrow and spend.
A tax charged on each litre of petrol and diesel.
An extra tax added on top of an existing tax.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget offers £100 energy payment, taxes banks and brings forward defence target
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget on 28 October 2026, offering households help with the cost of living while raising money from banks and gambling.
The government will pay £100 to 20 million households to help with winter energy bills. The 5p cut to fuel duty is extended for six months to 30 June 2027, tariffs are removed on over 100 food products, and the National Living Wage rises 3.9% to £13.21 an hour. Retail, hospitality and leisure firms get a two-year real-terms freeze in business rates.
To pay for it, the bank profits surcharge rises by 3 points to 6% and Machine Games Duty rises from 20% to 25%. Defence spending is to reach 3% of GDP by 2030, with £10 billion more for Ukraine. Ministers say the plan meets the fiscal rules, though CNBC reports that bond investors had wanted tighter spending.
levels.why: It shows how the government is balancing help for households against pressure from bond markets.

levels.headline: Healey's Budget: £100 energy payment, bank surcharge and defence pledge
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey used his first Budget on 28 October 2026 to offer cost of living support while raising revenue from banks and gambling.
Households get a £100 payment (20 million of them) towards winter energy bills. The 5p fuel duty cut runs for another six months, to 30 June 2027, and tariffs on over 100 food products are scrapped. The National Living Wage goes up 3.9% to £13.21. Retail, hospitality and leisure properties get a two-year real-terms freeze on business rates.
The bank profits surcharge rises by 3 points to 6% and Machine Games Duty goes from 20% to 25%. Defence spending is due to hit 3% of GDP in 2030 and Ukraine gets a further £10 billion. The government says it meets its fiscal rules, but CNBC notes investors wanted more cuts.
levels.why: Bond markets are watching closely, so the Budget affects borrowing costs for the whole country.

levels.headline: Budget gives families £100 for energy bills and raises taxes on banks
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, set out his first Budget on 28 October 2026. It gives families some help with living costs and asks banks and gambling firms to pay more.
About 20 million households will receive £100 towards winter energy bills. The 5p cut in fuel duty continues for six more months, and import taxes on over 100 foods, including chocolate and fruit juice, are removed. The National Living Wage, the minimum pay for adults, rises 3.9% to £13.21 an hour.
Banks will pay a higher surcharge on their profits, and the tax on gambling machines goes up. The Chancellor also promised to bring forward the target of spending 3% of national income on defence to 2030. The government says it is still following its own borrowing rules.
levels.why: It affects bills, pay and prices for millions of households.

levels.headline: Chancellor offers £100 towards winter energy bills in first Budget
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget on 28 October. He said it would give families breathing space and support businesses.
Households will get a £100 payment towards winter energy bills, reaching 20 million homes. The government will keep fuel duty 5p lower for another six months and remove tariffs from more than 100 food products. The National Living Wage will rise by 3.9% to £13.21 an hour, and shops, pubs and leisure businesses will see their business rates frozen in real terms for two years.
Banks will pay more tax on their profits, and Machine Games Duty rises to 25%. Defence spending will reach 3% of GDP by 2030, and Ukraine will get another £10 billion of support. Ministers insist the plans fit the fiscal rules, the limits they set on borrowing.
levels.why: Prices of energy, fuel and food are a worry for many families this winter.

levels.headline: The Budget: help with bills, paid for partly by banks
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, gave his first Budget speech on 28 October. A Budget is when the government says how it will raise and spend money.
The main help for families is a £100 payment to 20 million households for winter energy bills. Fuel duty, the tax on petrol and diesel, stays 5p lower for six more months. Tariffs, which are taxes on imports, are removed from over 100 foods. The minimum hourly wage for adults rises 3.9% to £13.21.
To raise money, banks will pay a bigger extra tax on profits, rising to 6%, and gambling machines will be taxed more. The government says it still obeys its own limits on borrowing, called fiscal rules, though some investors wanted deeper cuts.
levels.why: It shows who gets help and who pays more.

levels.headline: Budget gives £100 for energy bills and makes banks pay more
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey told Parliament how the government will raise and spend money. This is called the Budget, and it was on 28 October.
About 20 million homes will get £100 to help pay winter energy bills. Petrol and diesel will be taxed a little less for another six months. Some imported foods, such as chocolate and fruit juice, will no longer have extra taxes. The lowest legal hourly pay for adults will go up to £13.21.
Banks will pay more tax on their profits, and so will gambling machine firms. The government will also spend more on defence and give £10 billion to help Ukraine. It says it is not borrowing more than its rules allow, but some people who lend the government money wanted bigger savings.
levels.why: Costs of living and tax decisions touch every household.

levels.headline: The Budget: £100 off winter energy costs, more tax for banks
levels.body:
The Chancellor is the person in charge of the country's money. His name is John Healey, and on 28 October he explained his plans for taxes and spending.
Every year the government must decide how much tax to collect and what to spend it on. This time, it will give 20 million homes £100 for energy bills this winter. It will keep petrol and diesel tax lower for six months. Shops and pubs will not see their property tax go up for two years.
Banks will pay more tax on their profits. Gambling machines will also be taxed more. Pay for adults at the lowest legal level will rise to £13.21 an hour. The government says it can afford this and still follow its rules.
levels.why: The Budget decides how much help families get and who pays for it.

levels.headline: Budget: families get £100 to help with energy bills
levels.body:
On 28 October, a man called John Healey stood up in Parliament. He is the Chancellor, which means he looks after the country's money.
He told everyone what the government will do with taxes and spending. The government has a lot of money coming in from taxes. It must decide how to use it. Taxes are money that people and companies pay to the government.
Families will get £100 to help pay for heating and light this winter. Petrol will stay a bit cheaper for six months. Banks will have to pay more tax. The lowest pay for grown-ups will go up to £13.21 an hour. The government says it can pay for all this and not borrow too much.
levels.why: It decides who gets help with bills this winter.

levels.headline: Budget: a little help with bills this winter
levels.body:
Imagine your school has some money each year. The head teacher must decide what to buy and how much to ask parents to give. The government does this for the whole country.
This week, the man in charge of the country's money, John Healey, told everyone his plan. He said families will get £100 to help pay for heating and lights in the cold months. He also said banks must give a bit more of their money to the government.
He wants to make sure there is enough money for hospitals, schools and the army too. Some people think he should have saved more, but he says the plan is fair and the country can afford it.
levels.why: It is about sharing out the country's money fairly.

levels.headline: A big plan for the country's money
levels.body:
Think of a big family with one piggy bank. Once a year, someone has to decide how much to put in and how much to spend.
On 28 October, the person doing this for the whole country was called John Healey. He said that families would get £100 to help pay for warmth and light in winter. That is like getting a little extra pocket money when it is cold.
He also said that banks, which are places where people keep money, have to put a bit more into the piggy bank. The money helps pay for things we all share, like hospitals and schools. He says the plan is careful, so the piggy bank will not run empty.
levels.why: It helps families stay warm and shares out money for things we all use.

headline: S&P 500 falls 1.82% as tech selloff drags Nasdaq to worst day since June

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 large US companies.
An index dominated by technology company shares.
A company's forecast of how it expects to perform.

levels.headline: S&P 500 falls 1.82% as tech selloff drags Nasdaq to worst day since June
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on Friday 30 October 2026, the last completed trading session, falling 1.82% to 7,580.07.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to finish at 51,770.31, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.86% to 25,437.00, its worst day since June. The Nasdaq fell 2% over the week and 5.3% in October, and sits about 8% below its recent high.
Technology shares led the decline. Intel fell about 29% after weak guidance linked to softness in the PC market, its worst day since the 1970s, which cut roughly $12 billion from the value of the US government's stake. Amazon slipped about 1.4% after missing expectations for revenue and profit, with investors focused on negative free cash flow and heavy planned spending. Chipmakers also fell, with AMD down close to 11%.
levels.why: It signals investor nerves about big technology spending and affects pensions and savings.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends lower: S&P 500 down 1.82%, Nasdaq down 2.86%
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed lower on Friday 30 October 2026, the last completed session, down 1.82% at 7,580.07.
The Dow fell 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.31. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.86% to 25,437.00, its worst day since June, and ended October down 5.3%.
The selling started with company results. Intel lost about 29% after weak guidance tied to the PC market, and Amazon edged down about 1.4% after missing forecasts, with investors uneasy about its negative free cash flow and next year's large spending plans. Chipmakers also dropped, and AMD fell close to 11%. Defensive shares, which hold up better in downturns, did relatively well.
levels.why: Falling tech shares can drag on pension funds and investor confidence.

levels.headline: US shares fall sharply as investors dump tech stocks
levels.body:
US shares fell on Friday 30 October 2026, the latest completed trading day. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big US companies, closed down 1.82% at 7,580.07.
The Dow Jones index fell 1.09% to 51,770.31, and the Nasdaq, which is full of technology firms, dropped 2.86% to 25,437.00. That was its worst day since June.
Investors were worried by company news. Intel's shares plunged about 29% after it gave a weak forecast, its worst day since the 1970s. Amazon's shares dipped after its results fell short of expectations, and chip makers such as AMD also fell. The Nasdaq is now about 8% below its recent high and lost 5.3% over October.
levels.why: Share prices reflect confidence in the economy and affect savings and pensions.

levels.headline: Tech sell-off drags Wall Street lower
levels.body:
Wall Street had a bad day on Friday 30 October 2026. The S&P 500 index closed down 1.82% at 7,580.07, the most recent full trading day.
The Dow Jones fell 1.09% to 51,770.31 and the Nasdaq, which has many tech firms, fell 2.86% to 25,437.00, its worst day since June.
The biggest shock was Intel, whose shares dropped about 29% after it said sales might be weak because fewer people are buying PCs. That was Intel's worst day since the 1970s. Amazon's shares slipped after its latest results missed forecasts, and investors are watching how much cash it is spending. Over October, the Nasdaq lost 5.3%.
levels.why: Falling markets can hit pension pots and make companies more careful.

levels.headline: US shares fall after tech companies disappoint investors
levels.body:
US shares went down on Friday 30 October, the latest full day of trading. Shares are small parts of companies that people can buy and sell.
The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big firms, fell 1.82% to 7,580.07. The Dow fell 1.09% to 51,770.31. The Nasdaq, which has many technology firms, fell 2.86% to 25,437.00, its worst day since June.
Computer chip maker Intel lost about 29% of its value after saying its sales might be weak. Amazon's shares also dipped because its results were not as good as people had hoped. When people feel worried about companies, many sell at once and prices fall.
levels.why: Share prices matter to savers and pension holders.

levels.headline: US stock market falls as tech shares are dumped
levels.body:
Stock markets in the United States fell on Friday 30 October. A stock market is a place where people buy and sell small pieces of companies, called shares.
The S&P 500, a list of 500 big US firms, ended the day down 1.82%. The Dow, another list of big firms, fell 1.09%, and the Nasdaq, which is mostly tech firms, fell 2.86%. It was the Nasdaq's worst day since June.
Intel shares fell by about 29% after the company warned of weaker sales. Amazon's shares also dipped when its results disappointed investors. When many people sell shares at once, prices go down.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions and show how confident investors feel.

levels.headline: American shares fall on a bad day for tech firms
levels.body:
On Friday 30 October, share prices in the United States went down. Shares are small parts of a company that people can buy.
The S&P 500 is a group of 500 big companies, and its price fell by 1.82%. The Dow, another group, fell by 1.09%. The Nasdaq, where lots of technology companies are listed, fell by 2.86%. That was its worst day since June.
A firm called Intel, which makes computer chips, lost nearly a third of its value in one day because it warned that sales might be weak. Amazon's shares also fell a little after its results were not as good as people hoped. Many investors chose to sell, so prices dropped.
levels.why: It shows how nervous investors are about technology firms.

levels.headline: Shares fall in America after bad news from tech firms
levels.body:
Shares are tiny pieces of a company. People buy them hoping the company does well. On Friday 30 October, prices in the United States went down.
The S&P 500, which is a list of 500 big companies, fell by 1.82%. The Dow fell by 1.09%. The Nasdaq, a list full of technology companies, fell by 2.86%. It was its worst day since June.
Intel makes computer chips. It said it expects weak sales, and its share price dropped by almost 30%. Amazon, the online shop, also gave results that were worse than people expected. When people worry, many sell shares at the same time, and that pushes prices down.
levels.why: Lots of people's pensions are linked to share prices.

levels.headline: Why share prices went down in America
levels.body:
On Friday 30 October, lots of people in America sold shares. A share is a small piece of a company, a bit like owning one tiny slice of a big pizza.
The price of shares in 500 big companies went down by nearly 2 out of every 100. Shares in companies that make technology went down even more. One company, Intel, which makes computer chips, lost almost a third of its value.
This happened because Intel said it did not expect to sell as much. Amazon, the online shop, also did worse than people hoped. When people get worried, they sell, and prices fall.
levels.why: It shows how worried people are about big technology companies.

levels.headline: A bad day for big companies' shares
levels.body:
Imagine collecting football stickers. If everyone suddenly wants to swap theirs away, each sticker is worth less. Something like this happened on Friday in America.
People own tiny pieces of companies called shares. On Friday, many people sold shares in companies that make computers and technology. So the prices dropped, by almost 2 out of every 100 for the biggest 500 companies.
One firm that makes computer parts, Intel, said it would not sell as much as hoped. Its share price fell by nearly a third. The online shop Amazon also had news that was not as good as people wanted. People get nervous, and prices wobble.
levels.why: It shows how feelings can move prices, like swapping stickers.

headline: UK inflation climbs to 3.5% on fuel prices as Bank of England decision looms

terms.meaning: The yearly rise in the prices of a typical basket of goods and services.
The interest rate set by the Bank of England.
Inflation leaving out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco.

levels.headline: UK inflation climbs to 3.5% on fuel prices as Bank of England decision looms
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% economists expected, the Office for National Statistics said on 21 October.
Motor fuel inflation rose to 29.8% from 23.0%, with petrol up 8.2p a litre and diesel up 10.7p in a month, taking diesel to its highest since July 2022. Transport inflation was 6.6%, up from 4.6%. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, and CPIH was 3.6%.
The Bank of England has held Bank Rate at 3.75% since its December 2025 cut, with a 6-3 vote to hold in September. Markets widely expect a rise to 4% at the next decision on 5 November, which would be its first increase since 2023. The next inflation figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: A rate rise would raise costs for people with mortgages and loans.

levels.headline: Inflation rises to 3.5%; markets expect Bank of England to raise rates
levels.body:
UK inflation, measured by CPI, rose to 3.5% in the year to September 2026 from 3.1% in August, above the 3.4% forecast, according to the ONS.
Fuel was the main cause. Motor fuel inflation reached 29.8%, and diesel hit its highest price since July 2022. Core inflation, which strips out volatile items like energy and food, edged up to 2.8%.
The Bank of England has kept Bank Rate at 3.75% since December 2025, and in September three of nine policymakers voted for a rise to 4%. Economists quoted by Euronews say markets see a rise at the 5 November meeting as nearly certain, with a possible second increase before the end of the year. That would be the Bank's first hike since 2023.
levels.why: Higher borrowing costs and prices hit household budgets.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, and interest rates may go up next week
levels.body:
UK inflation, the yearly rise in prices, climbed to 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August. Economists had expected 3.4%, so the figure was a surprise.
Petrol and diesel prices drove most of the increase. Fuel prices were nearly 30% higher than a year earlier, and diesel hit its highest level since July 2022. Core inflation, which leaves out energy and food, rose to 2.8%.
The Bank of England sets interest rates to try to keep inflation under control. It has held its rate at 3.75% since December 2025, but markets now expect it to raise the rate to 4% on 5 November. That would be its first rise since 2023, and could mean higher mortgage and loan costs.
levels.why: It affects what you pay for goods, mortgages and loans.

levels.headline: Inflation rises to 3.5% as fuel costs jump
levels.body:
Prices across the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier, the Office for National Statistics reported. In August the figure was 3.1%.
The rise came mostly from fuel. Petrol went up by 8.2p a litre in a single month, and diesel by 10.7p, reaching its highest price since 2022. Costs linked to transport rose faster than anything else.
Because prices are rising, many experts think the Bank of England will increase its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4% at its meeting on 5 November. That would be the first rise since 2023. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, which can slow price rises, but they also raise mortgage payments for some households.
levels.why: Mortgage costs and shop prices may both be affected.

levels.headline: Inflation rises to 3.5% and the Bank of England may raise interest rates
levels.body:
Inflation, which means prices going up, was 3.5% in the UK in the year to September. In August it was 3.1%.
Most of the rise came from fuel. Petrol and diesel cost much more than a month earlier, and diesel was at its dearest since 2022. Higher fuel costs can make other goods dearer too, because things have to be delivered.
The Bank of England sets the interest rate, which is the cost of borrowing money. It is 3.75% now, and many people expect it to rise to 4% on 5 November. Raising it is meant to slow price rises, but it can make mortgages cost more.
levels.why: Price rises and interest rates both affect family budgets.

levels.headline: Prices rise faster, and interest rates could go up
levels.body:
Inflation is how fast prices rise. In September, UK prices were 3.5% higher than a year before. The month before, the figure was 3.1%.
Most of the extra rise came from fuel. Petrol and diesel got much more expensive in one month, and diesel reached its highest price since 2022. Higher fuel costs can push up the cost of moving goods, so other prices can rise too.
The Bank of England is in charge of the interest rate, the price of borrowing money. It is at 3.75% now. Many people expect it to go up to 4% on 5 November to help slow price rises. This would be the first rise since 2023, and might mean bigger mortgage payments.
levels.why: Rate rises change what households pay each month.

levels.headline: Prices go up faster, and borrowing may cost more
levels.body:
Prices in the UK in September were 3.5% higher than a year ago. This is called inflation. In August it was 3.1%.
The main reason was the cost of petrol and diesel, which jumped in one month. When fuel costs more, lorries and vans cost more to run, so shops may charge more too.
The Bank of England looks after the interest rate. This is the cost of borrowing money. It is 3.75% now. Many experts think the Bank will raise it to 4% on 5 November to slow down rising prices. If that happens, some people with mortgages will pay more each month, but saving money may pay a bit more too.
levels.why: It affects shopping bills, mortgages and savings.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster, so interest rates may rise
levels.body:
Inflation means prices going up. In September, things cost 3.5% more than a year earlier. A month earlier it was 3.1%.
A big reason was petrol and diesel, which cost much more. When fuel is dearer, it costs more to move food and goods around, so shops may charge more.
The Bank of England controls the interest rate. That is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or get when you save. Right now it is 3.75%. Many people think the Bank will raise it to 4% on 5 November to calm prices down. It has not done that since 2023. Families with mortgages could pay more.
levels.why: It could change what families pay for homes and shopping.

levels.headline: Why things cost more, and what the Bank might do
levels.body:
Inflation is when prices go up over time. A sweet that cost £1 last year might cost £1.03 or £1.04 now. Across the UK, prices rose 3.5% in a year.
The biggest reason this time was fuel. Petrol and diesel cost a lot more, and that makes lots of other things dearer too.
There is a bank for the whole country, called the Bank of England. It sets the interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. It is 3.75% now. Many people think it will go up to 4% on 5 November. This makes borrowing cost more, so people spend less and prices rise more slowly.
levels.why: It affects what people pay in shops and for loans.

levels.headline: Prices are rising, and a big bank may react
levels.body:
Think about the tuck shop. If the price of a snack goes up each month, your pocket money buys less. That is what inflation does, and across the UK prices rose 3.5% in a year.
Petrol and diesel cost a lot more this autumn, which pushes up other prices as well. So the grown-ups at the Bank of England, who look after the country's money, are thinking about what to do.
They might make borrowing money a bit dearer on 5 November. If people borrow less, prices may stop rising so fast. But it could also mean families with a mortgage have less left over each month.
levels.why: It can change how far a family's money goes.

headline: Burnham convenes first National Economic Council for the nations in Glasgow

terms.meaning: The governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, which handle many of their own affairs.
A group of firms, universities and researchers working in the same field in one area.
The head of the Scottish or Welsh government.

levels.headline: Burnham convenes first National Economic Council for the nations in Glasgow
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met the leaders of the devolved governments in Glasgow on 30 October 2026, convening the first National Economic Council meeting dedicated to the nations of the UK.
Scotland's First Minister John Swinney and Wales's First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth attended, with Northern Ireland also represented. Mr Burnham's message was to "work with me to empower every single part of the UK".
Afterwards he and Mr Swinney described the session as extremely positive, a valuable start to exploring how each government can contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and what they called good growth in every postcode.
The government also committed £1 billion through UK Research and Innovation over the next four years to support high-growth innovation clusters in priority sectors across the UK. The council was first set up in 2008 as a response to an economic emergency and has been revived under Mr Burnham.
levels.why: It shows how the UK government plans to share economic power with Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

levels.headline: PM meets Scottish and Welsh first ministers to start nations economic council
levels.body:
Andy Burnham chaired the first National Economic Council meeting for the nations of the UK in Glasgow on 30 October 2026.
John Swinney, First Minister of Scotland, and Rhun ap Iorwerth, First Minister of Wales, took part, and Northern Ireland sent representatives. The Prime Minister asked the devolved governments to work with him on regional empowerment.
Mr Burnham and Mr Swinney called the meeting extremely positive and a start to examining how each government can help with reindustrialisation and growth in every postcode.
Separately, the UK government pledged £1 billion over four years, through UK Research and Innovation, for innovation clusters in the sectors named in its Industrial Strategy. The National Economic Council dates back to 2008 and has been revived under the new Prime Minister.
levels.why: Cooperation between governments can shape jobs and investment across the UK.

levels.headline: Burnham meets devolved leaders in Glasgow to talk growth
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham held a meeting in Glasgow on 30 October with the leaders of the UK's devolved governments. These are the governments in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland that run many of their own services.
Scotland's First Minister John Swinney and Wales's First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth were there, and Northern Ireland was represented too. It was the first time the National Economic Council has met just for the nations.
Mr Burnham said he wants the governments to work together so that every part of the UK can grow. Mr Swinney agreed it was a positive start. The government also announced £1 billion over four years to help groups of innovative firms and researchers in different regions grow industries.
levels.why: It affects how money and decisions are shared across the four nations.

levels.headline: PM and first ministers meet to plan economic growth for every region
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Scotland's First Minister, John Swinney, and Wales's First Minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth, in Glasgow on 30 October. Northern Ireland also sent representatives.
The meeting was the first of the National Economic Council aimed at the UK's four nations. The Prime Minister said he wants the governments to work together to bring new industries and jobs to every area.
Afterwards he and Mr Swinney described the talks as extremely positive. Ministers also announced £1 billion over the next four years to support innovation clusters, which are places where businesses, universities and researchers work together on new ideas and technology.
levels.why: Better cooperation could bring jobs and investment to your area.

levels.headline: PM meets leaders of Scotland and Wales to talk about the economy
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met the leaders of Scotland and Wales in Glasgow on 30 October. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own governments, called devolved governments, which decide many things for themselves, such as parts of health and education.
The Scottish leader, John Swinney, and the Welsh leader, Rhun ap Iorwerth, joined him. Northern Ireland sent representatives.
They talked about how the governments can work together to help the economy grow in every area. Mr Burnham and Mr Swinney said the talks went very well. The UK government also said it will spend £1 billion over four years to help groups of new businesses and researchers, called innovation clusters, grow across the country.
levels.why: It is about sharing out power and money fairly across the UK.

levels.headline: Prime Minister meets Scottish and Welsh leaders to plan growth
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met the leaders of Scotland and Wales in Glasgow on 30 October. Northern Ireland sent people too.
These three places have their own governments, which decide many things for themselves. The Prime Minister wants all the governments to work together so that jobs and new businesses can grow in every part of the UK.
He and Scotland's leader, John Swinney, said the talks went very well. The UK government also said it will put £1 billion over four years into helping groups of businesses, universities and researchers work together on new ideas in different parts of the country.
levels.why: Working together can bring jobs and investment to more places.

levels.headline: PM talks with Scottish and Welsh leaders about jobs and growth
levels.body:
On 30 October, Prime Minister Andy Burnham met the leaders of Scotland and Wales in the city of Glasgow. Northern Ireland sent people too.
Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own government. These governments make many choices for their own area, but the UK government in London has a lot of power too. So they need to cooperate.
The leaders talked about how to make more jobs and help business grow in every part of the country. They said the meeting went well. The UK government also promised £1 billion over four years to help firms and scientists work together on new ideas in different areas.
levels.why: It shows how governments plan to work together for jobs.

levels.headline: Leaders from across the UK meet to plan for jobs
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, met two important leaders in Glasgow on 30 October. They were John Swinney, who leads Scotland's government, and Rhun ap Iorwerth, who leads Wales's government. People from Northern Ireland came too.
The UK has four parts: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Three of them have their own governments that decide some things for themselves. The Prime Minister said all the governments should work as a team so that new jobs and businesses can grow everywhere.
He said he would give £1 billion over four years to help new ideas and businesses. Mr Swinney said it was a good meeting.
levels.why: It is about making sure every place gets a fair chance.

levels.headline: Leaders of Scotland, Wales and the UK meet
levels.body:
The UK is made of four parts: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own small governments. They are a bit like class councils that decide some things for their own class.
On 30 October, the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, met the leaders of the Scottish and Welsh governments in Glasgow. People from Northern Ireland came too. They talked about how to help every place get more jobs and new businesses.
The Prime Minister said he wants everyone to work as a team. He also said £1 billion will be spent over four years to help new ideas grow. The leaders said it was a good meeting.
levels.why: It helps every part of the country get a fair share.

levels.headline: Grown-ups from different parts of the UK meet
levels.body:
Imagine a school with four classes. Each class has its own helper who decides some small things. The head teacher decides the big things. The UK is a bit like this.
On 30 October, the head of the whole UK government, Andy Burnham, met the leaders of the Scottish and Welsh helpers. They sat down in a city called Glasgow. They talked about how to make more jobs and help new businesses start everywhere.
The Prime Minister said all the leaders should work together, like a team. He also said some money, £1 billion, will be spent over four years to help people with new ideas. The leaders said the meeting was good.
levels.why: Working as a team helps everyone.

headline: Fed holds rates at 3.75% to 4% with two dissents for a hike, and markets price a December rise

terms.meaning: The central bank of the United States.
A rise in the central bank's main interest rate.
Elections held halfway through a US president's term to choose Congress.

levels.headline: Fed holds rates at 3.75% to 4% with two dissents for a hike, and markets price a December rise
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve left its main interest rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4% on 28 October 2026, days before the 3 November midterm elections.
Two officials, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, dissented because they wanted a quarter-point rise. The Fed had raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, and chair Warsh has said inflation is still too high.
US inflation was 3.7% in September, with energy prices lifted by the war involving Iran. After the decision, markets priced about an 80% to 87.5% chance of a quarter-point increase at the 8 to 9 December meeting. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said another rise would be needed soon, and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said at least two more quarter-point rises may be needed. Some observers question whether the timing around the election is politically neutral.
levels.why: US rates influence borrowing costs and markets around the world.

levels.headline: Fed pauses before midterms, but December hike looks likely
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve held its main rate at 3.75% to 4% on 28 October 2026. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-point increase.
The Fed raised rates in September, its first rise since 2023. With US inflation at 3.7% and energy prices high, officials including Alberto Musalem and Lorie Logan have said more hikes are needed. After the meeting, futures markets gave roughly an 80% to 87.5% chance of a quarter-point rise on 8 to 9 December.
The decision came days before the 3 November midterms, and some observers have speculated that officials would avoid acting so close to a vote. The Fed regards its political independence as a cornerstone.
levels.why: Central bank decisions affect mortgages, savings and the dollar.

levels.headline: US central bank holds interest rates but signals more rises may come
levels.body:
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, kept its main interest rate at 3.75% to 4% on 28 October 2026. Two members voted to raise it by a quarter of a percentage point instead.
The Fed had raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, because US inflation is 3.7%, well above its target, with fuel prices high. Several officials now say it will need to raise rates again. Markets think there is about an 80% to 87.5% chance of a rise at the 8 to 9 December meeting.
The vote came days before the midterm elections on 3 November. Some commentators wondered if that was why the Fed waited, but the Fed says it acts independently of politics.
levels.why: It affects borrowing costs and prices around the world.

levels.headline: Fed keeps rates on hold but a December rise looks likely
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve held US interest rates at 3.75% to 4% on 28 October. Two members, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, wanted to raise them by a quarter of a point.
The Fed put rates up in September for the first time since 2023. Inflation in the US is 3.7% and fuel is dear because of the war involving Iran. Several Fed officials say rates will need to rise again soon, and traders think there is roughly an 80% to 87.5% chance of a rise in December.
The decision came a few days before the US midterm elections on 3 November. The Fed says its decisions are independent of politics.
levels.why: The US rate affects loans, savings and the value of the dollar.

levels.headline: The US central bank pauses, but may raise rates in December
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve is the US central bank. On 28 October it decided not to change its main interest rate, which stays at 3.75% to 4%. The interest rate is the cost of borrowing money.
Two members wanted to raise it a bit. The Fed raised it in September, and prices in the US are going up at 3.7% a year, which is more than the Fed wants. Fuel costs are high because of a war involving Iran.
Several Fed officials say they will need to raise rates again. Traders think there is a high chance that will happen in December. The decision came a few days before elections on 3 November. The Fed says it does not make choices for political reasons.
levels.why: It affects how expensive loans are around the world.

levels.headline: US bank keeps interest rates the same, but may raise them soon
levels.body:
The US has a central bank called the Federal Reserve. It sets the interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. On 28 October, it kept the rate the same, at 3.75% to 4%.
Two people on the committee wanted to raise it. Prices in the US are going up by 3.7% a year, which is too fast for the Fed. Petrol and heating cost a lot because of a war involving Iran.
Several Fed leaders say rates will have to rise again. Many traders think that will happen in December. America also has big elections on 3 November. The Fed says it is not influenced by politics.
levels.why: It affects loans, savings and prices.

levels.headline: America's bank waits, but a rise may come
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve is the bank that looks after America's money. It decides the interest rate. That is the extra money people pay when they borrow, or get when they save.
On 28 October it did not change the rate. But two people on the team wanted to put it up. Prices in America are going up quite fast, by 3.7% in a year, so the bank wants to slow them. Fuel costs a lot because of a war.
Many people think the bank will raise the rate in December. There are also big elections in America on 3 November. Some people wondered if the bank was waiting for them. The bank says it is not.
levels.why: It affects what people pay to borrow money.

levels.headline: The US bank leaves its rate as it is
levels.body:
America has a bank for the whole country called the Federal Reserve. It decides how much extra people pay when they borrow money. This extra is called interest.
On 28 October the bank kept it the same. But prices in the shops in America have been going up fast. Petrol costs a lot because of a war. Some bank leaders think they will have to put the interest up soon, to stop prices rising so fast.
Many people think this will happen in December. America also has big elections on 3 November. The bank says it makes its choices without thinking about who might win.
levels.why: It matters to people who borrow or save.

levels.headline: The big bank in America decides to wait
levels.body:
A bank for a whole country decides how much extra people pay when they borrow money. In America, this bank is called the Federal Reserve.
On 28 October, the bank decided to wait and not change anything. It is like a teacher who says, let's wait a bit before we decide. But some of the grown-ups on the team wanted to make borrowing cost a bit more.
Prices in American shops have been going up fast, so they might do it in December. Voting day for important leaders is on 3 November. The bank says it does not pick sides.
levels.why: It can change how much families pay for loans.

levels.headline: A big bank decides to wait
levels.body:
Imagine a class piggy bank that lends money to children. If it asks for a little extra back, children borrow less.
In America, a big bank does this for the whole country. It is called the Federal Reserve. On 28 October the grown-ups there decided to wait and not change anything. But they said they may ask for a little extra soon.
They want to stop prices from going up too fast, so shops do not charge so much. Some people wanted to do it straight away. Now everyone is waiting to see what will happen in December.
levels.why: It helps keep prices from rising too quickly.

headline: Brent crude settles at $117.64, a six-month high, after Hormuz tanker attack and Houthi claims

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil.
A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman through which much of the world's oil is shipped.
West Texas Intermediate, the main US oil price benchmark.

levels.headline: Brent crude settles at $117.64, a six-month high, after Hormuz tanker attack and Houthi claims
levels.body:
Oil prices rose on Friday 30 October 2026. Brent crude, the international benchmark, settled at $117.64 a barrel, up 2.4% on the day and at a six-month high, while US benchmark WTI closed at $104.12.
For October, Brent gained 13.6% and WTI 15.2%, the fourth monthly rise in a row. Traders pointed to a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz that was hit by explosive devices attached by a small boat, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations body. Reports describe it as the first known successful limpet-mine strike in the waterway since the war with Iran began in February, and it was unclear who was responsible.
The Houthis also claimed attacks on sites in Saudi Arabia, including the Ras Tanura and Rabigh refineries and Abqaiq, claims that are unverified. Earlier in the week prices had eased on hopes of renewed US-Iran talks, after Iran received a letter from Vance.
levels.why: Oil prices feed straight into petrol, energy bills and inflation.

levels.headline: Oil jumps to six-month high on Hormuz attack and Houthi strike claims
levels.body:
Brent crude settled at $117.64 a barrel on Friday 30 October 2026, up 2.4% and its highest in six months. WTI settled at $104.12. Over October, Brent rose 13.6% and WTI 15.2%.
The jump followed an attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, where explosive devices were attached by a small boat, per the UKMTO. It is reported as the first known successful limpet-mine attack there since the war with Iran began in February, and nobody has been named as responsible.
Separately, the Houthis said they struck Saudi sites including the Ras Tanura and Rabigh refineries and Abqaiq. Those claims are unverified. Prices had earlier dipped on hopes of US-Iran talks, with Iran yet to reply to a letter from Vance.
levels.why: Higher oil prices push up fuel and energy costs worldwide.

levels.headline: Oil prices hit a six-month high as attacks raise fears for supply
levels.body:
Oil prices climbed on Friday 30 October 2026. Brent crude, the global benchmark, closed at $117.64 a barrel, its highest for six months. The US benchmark, WTI, closed at $104.12.
This was the fourth monthly gain in a row. In October Brent rose 13.6% and WTI 15.2%. A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea route for much of the world's oil, was damaged by explosives attached by a small boat. Nobody has said who did it.
The Houthis in Yemen also said they attacked several sites in Saudi Arabia, including refineries. That claim has not been confirmed. Earlier in the week, hopes of talks between the US and Iran had pulled prices down a little, but Iran has not replied to a letter from Vance.
levels.why: Fuel costs affect what you pay for petrol, food and heating.

levels.headline: Oil price jumps to six-month high on attack fears
levels.body:
Oil prices went up on Friday 30 October. Brent crude, the main world price, ended at $117.64 a barrel, the highest in six months. US oil, called WTI, ended at $104.12.
Over the whole month Brent rose 13.6%. Two things worried traders. First, a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route that much of the world's oil sails through, was hit by explosives stuck on by a small boat. Second, the Houthis, a group in Yemen, said they attacked oil sites in Saudi Arabia. That has not been confirmed.
Earlier in the week, hopes of talks between the US and Iran had calmed prices. A war involving Iran has been going on since February.
levels.why: Oil costs affect almost everything, from petrol to the price of food.

levels.headline: Oil gets dearer as attacks worry the market
levels.body:
The price of oil went up on Friday 30 October. A barrel of Brent crude, the main world price, cost $117.64 by the end of the day. That is the highest in six months. Over the month it went up by 13.6%.
Oil prices rise when people fear there will be less oil to buy. This week there were two scares. A tanker, which is a ship that carries oil, was hit by explosives in the Strait of Hormuz. This is a narrow stretch of sea that lots of oil ships use. A group called the Houthis also said they had attacked oil sites in Saudi Arabia, but nobody has proved this.
There has been a war with Iran since February, which is a big reason for high prices.
levels.why: Dearer oil means dearer petrol, flights and shopping.

levels.headline: Oil costs more after scares about ships and oil sites
levels.body:
Oil costs more again. On Friday 30 October, a barrel of the main world oil, called Brent, cost $117.64. That is the highest for six months. It rose by more than 13% over the whole month of October.
Prices go up when people worry that there will not be enough oil. This week, a ship carrying oil was hit by explosives in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow stretch of sea that lots of oil ships pass through. A group called the Houthis also said they had attacked oil sites in Saudi Arabia. Nobody has proved that yet.
A war involving Iran has been going on since February. Talks between the US and Iran might help, but Iran has not yet answered a letter.
levels.why: It makes petrol, heating and many other things cost more.

levels.headline: Oil gets more expensive after ship attack
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid that comes from under the ground. We use it to make petrol for cars and to make plastic. When oil costs more, lots of other things cost more too.
On Friday 30 October, a barrel of oil cost $117.64. That is more than it has cost for six months. Over October, the price went up by more than 13%.
One reason is that a ship carrying oil was damaged by explosives in a narrow sea passage called the Strait of Hormuz. Many oil ships go that way. A group called the Houthis also said they attacked places in Saudi Arabia that make oil. People are worried that there will be less oil to go round. A war with Iran began in February.
levels.why: Oil prices change what we pay for petrol and food.

levels.headline: Why oil costs more this week
levels.body:
Oil is a liquid found underground. We use it to make petrol for cars and lorries. When there is less oil to go round, it costs more.
This week, oil got more expensive. A big ship that carries oil was damaged by a bomb in a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. A lot of the world's oil goes through there. A group called the Houthis also said they had attacked oil places in a country called Saudi Arabia.
Because people are scared there will be less oil, they paid more for it. A barrel of oil cost $117.64 on Friday. When oil costs more, petrol and many other things cost more too.
levels.why: It makes everyday things more expensive.

levels.headline: Oil costs more because of worries about ships
levels.body:
Oil is a thick black liquid that comes from under the ground. It is used to make petrol, which makes cars go. When there is not enough, the price goes up, like when everyone wants the last cake at a party.
This week, a big ship carrying oil was hurt by a bomb in a narrow sea path. Lots of oil ships use that path. Some people also said they attacked places that make oil in Saudi Arabia. Now people worry there will not be enough oil. So it costs more.
When oil costs more, petrol costs more, and the shops may charge more too.
levels.why: It can make petrol and food cost more.

levels.headline: Oil is getting more expensive
levels.body:
Imagine everyone in school wants the same toy. The toy gets harder to find, so it costs more. This happens with oil too.
Oil is a thick black liquid from under the ground. It is used to make petrol for cars and lorries. This week, a ship carrying oil was damaged by a bomb. Some people also said they attacked places that make oil.
Now people are worried there will be less oil. So the price went up to the highest in six months. When oil costs more, petrol costs more, and things in the shops can cost more too. Grown-ups hope talks between countries can help.
levels.why: It makes things cost more for families.

headline: UK brings forward 3% defence target to 2030 and pledges extra £10 billion for Ukraine

terms.meaning: A military alliance of countries in Europe and North America.
A promise that the government will cover a loss if a foreign buyer fails to pay a British exporter.
A government exercise that sets budgets for departments over several years.

levels.headline: UK brings forward 3% defence target to 2030 and pledges extra £10 billion for Ukraine
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey used the 28 October 2026 Budget to bring forward Britain's defence spending target and to promise more help for Ukraine.
The UK now aims to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, while keeping the NATO commitment of 3.5% by 2035. The Chancellor announced an extra £10 billion in economic and military support for Ukraine, mostly delivered through loans and export finance guarantees, and £500 million in urgent winter military funding.
The government says it will set out how it will pay for the defence targets at next year's spending review, so the detail of the funding is still pending.
The decision follows heavy pressure on European governments to spend more on their armed forces as the war in Ukraine continues. CNBC presents the defence target and the Ukraine pledge together in its report on the Budget.
levels.why: It sets how much the UK spends on its armed forces and on supporting Ukraine.

levels.headline: Healey sets 2030 date for 3% defence spending and adds £10bn for Ukraine
levels.body:
In the 28 October Budget, Chancellor John Healey brought the UK's goal of spending 3% of GDP on defence forward to 2030. The NATO target of 3.5% by 2035 stays in place.
He also announced an additional £10 billion of economic and military support for Ukraine, mostly through loans and export finance guarantees, together with £500 million of urgent winter military funding.
The government has said it will explain how the defence targets will be paid for at next year's spending review. Until then, how the extra spending is funded remains unclear. The announcements come as European countries face pressure to strengthen their armed forces while the war in Ukraine continues.
levels.why: Defence spending competes with other priorities such as health and benefits.

levels.headline: UK promises to spend more on defence sooner and helps Ukraine with £10 billion
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, said in the Budget on 28 October that the UK will spend 3% of its national income on defence by 2030. That is earlier than planned. The NATO goal of 3.5% by 2035 still stands.
He also promised another £10 billion to help Ukraine, mostly through loans and guarantees that help British firms export goods. There is a further £500 million for urgent military needs over the winter.
The government says it will explain how to pay for the defence plans at next year's spending review. That is when it sets budgets for each department over several years. Critics will want to know what other spending might be reduced.
levels.why: It shows how the UK is responding to threats and to the war in Ukraine.

levels.headline: Budget brings forward defence goal and gives Ukraine more help
levels.body:
The UK will spend 3% of its national income on defence by 2030, the Chancellor said in the Budget on 28 October. The aim of reaching 3.5% by 2035, agreed with NATO, remains.
John Healey also announced £10 billion of extra help for Ukraine, mostly loans and export guarantees, plus £500 million of urgent military support for the winter.
The government says details of how it will pay for the defence target will come at next year's spending review. The announcement comes as European governments face pressure to do more for their own security while the war in Ukraine continues.
levels.why: Defence choices affect taxes, spending and security.

levels.headline: UK to spend more on defence sooner and give Ukraine £10 billion
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, said on 28 October that the UK will spend 3% of everything the country earns on defence by 2030. This is sooner than before. The UK has also promised NATO, a group of allies, that it will reach 3.5% by 2035.
He also announced £10 billion more to help Ukraine. Most of it will be loans and guarantees to help British firms sell goods abroad. There is also £500 million for urgent military needs this winter.
The government has not yet said exactly how it will pay for it all. It plans to explain at next year's spending review, when it decides how much each part of government gets.
levels.why: It affects how safe the country is and how tax money is used.

levels.headline: The UK will spend more on defence sooner and help Ukraine
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, said on 28 October that the UK will spend 3% of what the country earns on defence by 2030. Defence means the armed forces that protect the country. The UK has also agreed with its NATO allies to reach 3.5% by 2035.
He also said £10 billion more will go to help Ukraine, which is fighting a war with Russia. Most of it will be loans and guarantees that help British firms sell goods abroad. A further £500 million is for urgent military needs this winter.
The government has not yet said exactly how it will pay for all this. It says it will explain next year.
levels.why: Defence spending affects both safety and what is left for other services.

levels.headline: UK plans to spend more on its army and help Ukraine
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, said the UK will spend more on defence. Defence means the army, navy and air force, which protect the country.
By 2030, the UK wants to spend 3 out of every 100 pounds that the country earns on defence. It has also promised friends in NATO, a group of allied countries, to reach 3.5 by 2035.
He also said £10 billion more will go to help Ukraine, a country fighting a war with Russia. Most of that will be loans and promises to help British firms sell things abroad. The government says it will explain how to pay for everything next year.
levels.why: Money spent on defence cannot be spent on other things.

levels.headline: The UK will spend more on defence and help Ukraine
levels.body:
The Chancellor is the person in charge of the country's money. His name is John Healey. On 28 October, he said the UK would spend more on defence, which means keeping the country safe with soldiers, ships and planes.
The UK wants to reach 3% of what the country earns by 2030. Later, it wants 3.5%, because it agreed this with its allies in NATO.
He also promised £10 billion to help Ukraine, which is fighting a war with Russia. Some of it is loans. The government has not yet said exactly where all the money will come from. It will tell us next year.
levels.why: It is about safety, and about how money gets shared.

levels.headline: The UK will spend more to stay safe
levels.body:
Countries have soldiers, ships and planes to keep people safe. This is called defence. It costs a lot of money.
The man who looks after the UK's money is called the Chancellor. His name is John Healey. On 28 October he said that the UK will spend more on defence, and sooner than planned. He also said the UK will give more help to Ukraine. Ukraine is a country that is in a war with Russia.
The help is worth £10 billion. Most of it is loans, which means Ukraine has to pay it back one day. The government will say next year where all the money will come from.
levels.why: It is about keeping people safe and helping a country in need.

levels.headline: Spending money to keep people safe
levels.body:
A school has rules and helpers to keep children safe. A country does this too, with soldiers, ships and planes. This costs money.
The person who looks after the UK's money, John Healey, said the UK will spend more on keeping safe. He also said the UK will help a country called Ukraine, which is in a long fight with another country.
Some of the help is like lending a friend money for their lunch. They have to pay it back later. The grown-ups still need to work out where all the money will come from, and they will tell everyone next year.
levels.why: It shows how a country looks after its own people and its friends.

headline: Burnham does not rule out manifesto pledge to rejoin EU but says referendum not right now

terms.meaning: An area where goods, services, money and people move freely between member countries.
An agreement where countries charge the same taxes on goods from outside.
A party's published list of promises before an election.

levels.headline: Burnham does not rule out manifesto pledge to rejoin EU but says referendum not right now
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is "possible" a future election manifesto could include a referendum on rejoining the EU, though he told the BBC a referendum "wouldn't be the right thing to do right now".
He has described rejoining as one option among several: staying as things are, a customs union, the single market, or going "all the way". He is due to set out these options around a UK-EU summit.
Mr Burnham has said he is bound by Keir Starmer's 2024 manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union. He has also said he cannot see himself recommending joining the euro or the Schengen borderless area.
A YouGov survey suggested 56% of British voters would back rejoining, but Euronews notes the move could alienate Labour voters who supported Brexit and push some towards the Conservatives or Reform UK. The next general election is not expected before 2029.
levels.why: It could decide the UK's long-term relationship with its biggest trading partner.

levels.headline: Burnham leaves door open to EU referendum pledge at next election
levels.body:
Andy Burnham told the BBC it was "possible" a referendum on rejoining the EU could appear in a future manifesto, but said holding one now would not be right.
He has listed his options as the status quo, a customs union, the single market or going "all the way", and will set them out near a UK-EU summit. Yet he has committed to the 2024 Labour manifesto, which ruled out free movement, the single market and a customs union, and said he does not see the UK joining the euro or Schengen.
A YouGov poll put support for rejoining at 56%. Euronews says there is political risk, as Leave-voting Labour supporters could drift to the Conservatives or Reform UK. Officials suggest the 2029 election could test public support.
levels.why: The question affects trade, travel, jobs and the next election.

levels.headline: Burnham says EU referendum pledge is possible, but not yet
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said a pledge to hold a referendum on rejoining the EU could be in a future Labour manifesto, but that a vote now would be wrong.
He has set out several choices for the UK's relationship with Europe: keep things as they are, join a customs union, rejoin the single market, or go all the way and rejoin. He plans to explain more around a UK-EU summit.
For now he says he will stick to the 2024 manifesto, which rules out a customs union, the single market and free movement of people. A poll by YouGov found 56% of voters would back rejoining. However, some Labour voters backed Brexit, so the issue is risky for the party. The next election is expected in 2029.
levels.why: It could change trade, travel and work rules between the UK and Europe.

levels.headline: PM keeps rejoining the EU on the table but rules out a referendum for now
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says a referendum on rejoining the EU is "possible" in a future manifesto but would not be right at the moment.
He has listed possible routes for relations with the EU, from staying as things are to joining a customs union or the single market, or going "all the way". He will set these out around a UK-EU summit.
He says he is tied to Labour's 2024 manifesto, which rules out free movement, the single market and a customs union, and that he would not recommend joining the euro or Schengen. A YouGov poll found 56% of voters support rejoining, but Euronews notes the risk of losing Leave-backing Labour voters to the Conservatives or Reform UK. A general election is not expected before 2029.
levels.why: The UK's ties with Europe affect prices, jobs and travel.

levels.headline: Burnham says rejoining the EU is possible one day, but not now
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that rejoining the European Union could one day be in his party's election promises, called a manifesto. But he said a vote on it now would be wrong.
He has said there are several choices. The UK could keep things as they are. It could join a customs union, which means charging the same import taxes as the EU. It could rejoin the single market, which lets goods and services move freely. Or it could go all the way and rejoin.
He says he will stick to promises from 2024 that rule out some of these. A poll found 56% of people would back rejoining. But some Labour voters wanted Brexit, so it is a risk. The next election is expected in 2029.
levels.why: It may affect trade, prices and travel to Europe.

levels.headline: The PM says rejoining the EU is possible one day, not now
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that his party could one day promise a vote on rejoining the European Union. He said this is possible, but that a vote now would not be right.
He has listed choices for the UK's future with Europe, from keeping things as they are to joining a customs union or the single market, or rejoining fully. He says he will keep to promises made in 2024 that rule out some of these.
A poll found that 56% of voters would back rejoining. But some Labour voters wanted to leave the EU, so the question is risky for his party. The next election is not expected before 2029.
levels.why: It could change trade, travel and work between the UK and Europe.

levels.headline: PM says UK could rejoin the EU one day but no vote yet
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it is possible that his party might promise a vote on rejoining the EU before the next election. But he said now is not the right time for a vote.
The UK left the EU in 2020 after a vote in 2016. Since then, people have argued about whether it was a good idea. Mr Burnham has listed choices: stay as things are, join a customs union, rejoin the single market, or rejoin fully. He will say more later.
He says he must keep promises made in 2024 that ruled out some of these. A poll found 56% of voters would like to rejoin. But some Labour voters wanted to leave the EU, so it is a hard choice. The next election is not expected before 2029.
levels.why: It is a big decision about the UK's place in the world.

levels.headline: The PM says rejoining the EU is an option, but not right now
levels.body:
The UK used to be in a group of countries called the European Union, or EU. It left in 2020. Some people want to go back, and some do not.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that one day, his party might promise a vote on going back. But he said it is not the right time yet. He listed choices, from staying as things are to joining fully again.
He also said he would keep promises his party made in 2024, which rule out some choices. A poll said 56 out of 100 people would like to rejoin. But some people who voted for his party wanted to leave, so he must be careful. The next big election will be in 2029 or later.
levels.why: It could change how we trade and travel.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister talks about the UK and Europe
levels.body:
The UK used to belong to a club of European countries, called the EU. It left a few years ago. Some people miss the club and some are glad to be out.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said the UK might one day vote on whether to go back. He did not say it would happen. He said the time is not right yet.
He has a list of choices, from staying as we are to joining the club again completely. He is thinking about them. A survey found that just over half of people, 56 in every 100, would like to go back. But some people would be upset, so he has to think carefully.
levels.why: It is a big choice about friends and trade.

levels.headline: Should the UK rejoin a club of countries?
levels.body:
Imagine your class used to be in a club with the other classes. Then your class left the club. Some children were happy and some were sad.
Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says his party might one day ask people if they want to join the club again. He said that is possible, but not now. He is thinking about different choices, like joining a little or joining fully.
He asked a lot of people, and just over half said yes to rejoining. But some did not. So he wants to be careful, and he will not make a big decision in a hurry.
levels.why: It is about which friends and trading partners the UK has.

headline: ECB holds deposit rate at 2.5% as Lagarde announces she will leave early

terms.meaning: The ECB's main interest rate, paid on money banks deposit with it.
The ECB's main decision-making body.
The group of EU countries that use the euro.

levels.headline: ECB holds deposit rate at 2.5% as Lagarde announces she will leave early
levels.body:
The European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2.5% on 29 October 2026, after two rate rises this year. The Governing Council considered raising rates but decided unanimously to hold.
President Christine Lagarde said policy was "well positioned enough at this stage to hold", while suggesting a December move is possible. Eurozone inflation is 3.8%, almost double the 2% target, with energy prices linked to the Iran war a key factor. Average 10-year eurozone government bond yields have risen by around 35 basis points since the September projections, and bond market stress in France is another concern.
Ms Lagarde also announced that she will step down on 7 February, ahead of the end of her term in October 2027. Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot are seen as frontrunners to succeed her. Markets expect a hike by December.
levels.why: The ECB's rates affect borrowing costs across the eurozone.

levels.headline: ECB leaves rates at 2.5%, December hike in play, Lagarde to depart in February
levels.body:
The ECB kept its deposit rate at 2.5% on 29 October 2026, after raising rates twice this year. Policymakers discussed a rise but voted unanimously to hold.
Christine Lagarde said policy was "well positioned enough at this stage to hold" and listed the data due before the December meeting. Inflation in the euro area is 3.8%, nearly twice the 2% target, partly because of energy costs tied to the Iran war. Bond yields have risen about 35 basis points since September, and stress in French bonds is a worry.
Ms Lagarde will leave on 7 February, earlier than her October 2027 term end. Pablo Hernández de Cos and Klaas Knot are seen as frontrunners to replace her. Markets price a rise by December.
levels.why: A leadership change at the ECB comes just as policy gets harder.

levels.headline: European Central Bank holds rates and Lagarde says she will step down early
levels.body:
The European Central Bank kept its main interest rate at 2.5% on 29 October 2026. It has raised rates twice this year, and members discussed a third rise but all agreed to wait.
President Christine Lagarde said the bank was in a good enough position to hold, but hinted that a December rise is possible. Inflation across the eurozone is 3.8%, almost double the 2% target, because of high energy prices linked to the war involving Iran.
She also said she will leave on 7 February, earlier than her term required, which ends in October 2027. Pablo Hernández de Cos of Spain and Klaas Knot of the Netherlands are seen as the likeliest successors. Markets expect another rise by December.
levels.why: Interest rates in Europe affect loans, savings and prices.

levels.headline: ECB holds interest rates, and Lagarde will leave early
levels.body:
The European Central Bank kept its main interest rate at 2.5% on 29 October. It has raised the rate twice this year, and members talked about a third rise but chose to wait.
Christine Lagarde, the bank's president, said the bank was well placed to wait, but a rise in December is possible. Prices in the eurozone are rising at 3.8% a year, nearly double the 2% target, and high energy costs from the war involving Iran are a big reason.
Ms Lagarde said she will leave her job on 7 February, earlier than planned. Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot are seen as the most likely replacements.
levels.why: It affects the cost of loans across the eurozone.

levels.headline: Europe's central bank waits, and its boss will leave early
levels.body:
The European Central Bank looks after money for countries that use the euro. On 29 October it kept its main interest rate at 2.5%. The interest rate is the price of borrowing money.
It had raised the rate twice this year. This time everyone agreed to wait, but Christine Lagarde, the bank's president, said a rise in December is possible. Prices are going up by 3.8% a year, which is almost double what the bank wants. High energy costs because of a war involving Iran are a big reason.
Ms Lagarde also said she will leave her job early, on 7 February. People are talking about who might take over.
levels.why: It affects loans and prices across Europe.

levels.headline: Europe's bank waits on interest rates, and its leader says goodbye
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe use the same money, the euro. They share a bank, called the European Central Bank. It decides the interest rate, which is the extra money people pay when they borrow.
On 29 October, the bank kept the rate at 2.5%. It had raised the rate twice already this year. Prices are going up faster than the bank wants, partly because energy costs a lot after a war involving Iran. The bank might raise the rate again in December.
The bank's boss, Christine Lagarde, also said she will leave on 7 February. That is earlier than planned. Other people are now being talked about to take over.
levels.why: It affects the cost of borrowing for many families.

levels.headline: Europe's central bank holds rates and its president will go early
levels.body:
The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the countries that use the euro, kept its main rate at 2.5% on 29 October. The interest rate is the price of borrowing money.
The bank had raised the rate twice this year. Prices in the eurozone are rising by 3.8% a year, nearly double its 2% aim, partly because of high energy costs. It chose to wait this time, but it said a rise in December is possible.
The bank's president, Christine Lagarde, said she will leave on 7 February, earlier than planned. People are talking about who might take over. Two names mentioned are Pablo Hernández de Cos of Spain and Klaas Knot of the Netherlands.
levels.why: It affects loans and prices in many European countries.

levels.headline: Europe's money bank keeps its rate the same
levels.body:
Lots of countries in Europe use the same coins and notes, called the euro. They share one bank to look after their money. It is called the European Central Bank.
On 29 October, the bank decided to keep the cost of borrowing at 2.5%. That is the extra money people pay when they borrow. Prices have been going up fast, and the bank is worried. It might raise the cost of borrowing in December.
The boss of the bank, a woman named Christine Lagarde, said she will leave her job early, in February. People are now talking about who will take over.
levels.why: It matters to people who borrow or save in euros.

levels.headline: The bank for euro countries waits
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe use the same money, the euro. They have one big bank to look after it. It decides how much extra people pay when they borrow money.
On 29 October, the bank decided to wait and keep things the same. Prices in the shops have been going up quite fast, and the bank wants to slow that down. It may make borrowing cost more in December.
The boss of the bank, Christine Lagarde, said she will leave in February. That is a bit earlier than planned. Other people have been named as possible new bosses.
levels.why: It helps keep prices from rising too fast.

levels.headline: A big bank waits and its boss will leave
levels.body:
Lots of countries in Europe share the same money. They also share one big bank for it. The bank decides whether borrowing money should cost more or less.
On 29 October the grown-ups at the bank decided to wait. They may change their mind in December. Prices in the shops have been going up quite fast, and the bank wants to slow them down.
The boss of the bank, Christine Lagarde, said she will leave her job early. She will go in February. Other people are being talked about as the next boss, a bit like choosing a new head teacher.
levels.why: It helps keep shop prices steady.

headline: EU to fast-track second €45 billion Ukraine tranche as it searches for ways to fill a €70 billion gap

terms.meaning: One instalment of a loan paid out in stages.
Money borrowed together by several countries, which they repay together.
The difference between money needed and money available.

levels.headline: EU to fast-track second €45 billion Ukraine tranche as it searches for ways to fill a €70 billion gap
levels.body:
The European Commission is bringing forward the second €45 billion instalment of its €90 billion loan to Ukraine, according to a strategy published on Friday 30 October 2026.
The tranche is split into €31.7 billion for military needs and €13.3 billion for Ukraine's budget, with funds concentrated in the first half of 2027 to avoid a cut-off of assistance. For 2026, Brussels intends to transfer €45 billion in stages, €16.7 billion of it financial support and €28.3 billion military, with some already paid.
Ukraine faces a funding shortfall of about €70 billion next year. Officials insist the EU will cover no more than two-thirds, roughly €46 billion, leaving the rest to other allies, and joint debt is the frontrunner to plug the hole. Payments depend on reforms, and Brussels has pressed Kyiv to move faster.
levels.why: It shows how far Europe will go to keep Ukraine's government and army funded.

levels.headline: Brussels pulls forward €45bn for Ukraine amid acute funding squeeze
levels.body:
The Commission said on 30 October 2026 that it will fast-track the second €45 billion tranche of the €90 billion loan for Ukraine, concentrating the money in the first half of 2027.
The tranche splits into €31.7 billion for the military and €13.3 billion for the budget. In 2026, €45 billion is being paid in stages, €16.7 billion as financial support and €28.3 billion for the military.
Ukraine still faces a roughly €70 billion shortfall next year. Officials say the EU will cover no more than two-thirds, about €46 billion, with the rest from other allies, and joint debt is the likely tool. Payments are linked to reforms, and Brussels has urged Kyiv to speed them up.
levels.why: Funding decisions shape how long Ukraine can keep fighting and running public services.

levels.headline: EU speeds up €45 billion in loans for Ukraine as money runs short
levels.body:
The EU is speeding up the second €45 billion instalment of a €90 billion loan to Ukraine, the European Commission said on 30 October 2026.
Of this, €31.7 billion is for military needs and €13.3 billion is for Ukraine's budget. Most of the money will be paid in the first half of 2027 so help is not cut off. This year, €45 billion is being sent in stages, and some has already been paid.
Ukraine expects to be about €70 billion short next year. The EU says it will cover no more than two-thirds of that, about €46 billion, and other allies must find the rest. Joint borrowing by EU countries is the leading way to fill the gap. Ukraine must keep making reforms to receive the money.
levels.why: It matters for Ukraine's survival and for Europe's security.

levels.headline: EU moves faster to send €45 billion to Ukraine
levels.body:
The European Commission announced on 30 October that it will pay out the second €45 billion of its €90 billion loan to Ukraine sooner than planned.
Most of it, €31.7 billion, is for military needs, and €13.3 billion is for Ukraine's government budget. The money will mostly arrive in the first half of 2027. In 2026, a further €45 billion is being paid in stages.
Ukraine is expected to be about €70 billion short next year. The EU says it will provide no more than two-thirds of that, about €46 billion, and other allies must supply the rest. Borrowing together as a group of countries, called joint debt, is the most likely way. Ukraine also has to carry on with reforms.
levels.why: It affects how well Ukraine can pay for its army and services.

levels.headline: EU brings forward €45 billion of loans for Ukraine
levels.body:
The European Union will send Ukraine the next €45 billion of its €90 billion loan sooner than planned, the European Commission said on 30 October.
Most of it, €31.7 billion, is for the military, and €13.3 billion is for the government's budget. The money will mostly be paid in the first half of 2027 so that help is not cut off.
