Ukraine expects to be about €70 billion short next year. The EU says it will cover no more than two-thirds, around €46 billion, and other allies must supply the rest. Countries borrowing together, known as joint debt, is the most likely method. The loans depend on Ukraine keeping up its reforms.
levels.why: Ukraine's army and public services depend on this money.

levels.headline: EU speeds up money for Ukraine
levels.body:
The European Union has decided to send Ukraine a large amount of money sooner than planned. The Commission, the EU's executive body, said so on 30 October.
The money is a loan, paid in parts called tranches. The next tranche is €45 billion. Most of it, €31.7 billion, is for the army, and the rest helps the government pay for services. It will mostly be paid in the first half of 2027.
Ukraine expects to be about €70 billion short next year. The EU says it will pay up to two-thirds, and others must pay the rest. EU countries may borrow together to find the money. Ukraine must also keep making reforms.
levels.why: Ukraine needs money to keep its army and public services going.

levels.headline: EU speeds up a big loan to Ukraine
levels.body:
The EU is a group of European countries. On 30 October, its Commission said it will send Ukraine a large loan sooner than planned. A loan is money that has to be paid back.
The next part of the loan is worth €45 billion. Most of it is for Ukraine's army. The rest helps the government pay for things like wages and services. Ukraine is fighting a war with Russia, and war costs a lot.
Ukraine thinks it will be about €70 billion short next year. The EU says it can cover about two-thirds of that. Other friends must help with the rest. Ukraine has to keep making changes to earn the money.
levels.why: It helps Ukraine pay for its army and for public services.

levels.headline: EU to send Ukraine money sooner
levels.body:
The European Union, or EU, is a group of countries in Europe. It has promised to lend Ukraine a lot of money. Ukraine is fighting a war with Russia, and the war costs a great deal.
On 30 October, the EU said it would send the next part of the money sooner. That part is worth €45 billion. Some of it is for soldiers and weapons. The rest helps the government pay people who work for it, such as teachers and nurses.
Ukraine thinks it will not have enough money next year. The EU says it will give most of what is missing. It wants other friends to give the rest too.
levels.why: It helps Ukraine stay safe and keep its services running.

levels.headline: Europe will lend Ukraine money sooner
levels.body:
Ukraine is a country in a long war. It needs a lot of money for its army and for schools and hospitals.
Europe's group of countries, called the EU, promised to lend a lot of money. On 30 October, it said it would give the next part sooner. That part is worth €45 billion. A billion is a thousand millions, so this is a huge amount.
Ukraine still thinks it will be short of money next year. The EU says it can find about two-thirds of what is missing. Other friends need to give the rest. Ukraine has also promised to make some changes.
levels.why: Ukraine needs help to keep its people safe.

levels.headline: Europe plans to help Ukraine with money
levels.body:
Think of a friend whose family is in trouble. You lend them some of your pocket money so they can buy food. This is a bit like what Europe is doing for Ukraine.
Ukraine is in a war and needs money for its soldiers, hospitals and schools. Many countries in Europe joined together to lend a lot of money. On 30 October, they said they would send the next part earlier.
But Ukraine still needs more money next year. Europe will give most of it, and other friends will be asked to help with the rest.
levels.why: It helps a country in trouble.

headline: First residents leave Russian-occupied Oleshky under US-brokered local ceasefire

terms.meaning: An agreement to stop fighting, at least for a time.
Under the control of foreign forces.
Moving people out of a dangerous place.

levels.headline: First residents leave Russian-occupied Oleshky under US-brokered local ceasefire
levels.body:
A local ceasefire in Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city in Ukraine's Kherson region, has allowed aid in and the first civilians out, with evacuees reaching Ukraine on 31 October 2026.
The White House said both sides agreed to halt military action in the city, with a truce reported as lasting until 1 November, and credited Melania Trump with brokering it. A convoy of 25 buses and ambulances brought food and medicine. Evacuees travelled by bus via Crimea to the Russian town of Anapa, flew to Belarus and crossed into Ukraine in the Chernihiv region.
Estimates of those remaining range from about 1,700 to 2,000. Critics question whether leaving is voluntary, since Ukrainian-held land is only a few kilometres across the Dnipro. Former Ukrainian prime minister Yatsenyuk said the truce would not lead to a wider one, while Russia's ombudsman said few residents wanted to leave.
levels.why: It is a rare humanitarian pause in a war, but doubts remain about its terms.

levels.headline: Oleshky truce lets aid in and civilians out, but the route raises concerns
levels.body:
A temporary ceasefire in the occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has allowed humanitarian aid in and the start of civilian evacuations, with the first evacuees arriving in Ukraine on 31 October 2026.
The White House says both Russia and Ukraine agreed to stop military action, and credits Melania Trump. Reports differ on the start, but the truce is due to last until about 1 November. A convoy of 25 buses and ambulances delivered food and medicine.
Evacuees went via Crimea to Anapa in Russia, flew to Belarus, then crossed into Chernihiv. Ukrainian officials say about 1,700 people remained; Euronews says about 2,000. Critics say the route raises doubts about whether leaving is truly voluntary. Yatsenyuk called the Russian approach treating residents as hostages.
levels.why: Civilians in occupied areas depend on such deals for food, medicine and safe passage.

levels.headline: Civilians leave besieged Oleshky during a short ceasefire
levels.body:
A short ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has let aid in and the first residents out. The first evacuees reached Ukraine on 31 October.
The White House said Russia and Ukraine had both agreed to stop military action in the city and credited Melania Trump with brokering the deal. The truce is expected to last until about 1 November. Buses and ambulances brought food and medicine.
The people who left were taken by bus through Crimea to Anapa in Russia, flown to Belarus, and then crossed into Ukraine. Roughly 1,700 to 2,000 people remain. Critics worry about the long route through Russia and say it is unclear that everyone leaving is doing so by choice. A former Ukrainian prime minister said the pause will not lead to peace.
levels.why: It affects people trapped in a war zone, and shows how fragile peace efforts are.

levels.headline: Short ceasefire lets some people leave Oleshky
levels.body:
A short ceasefire has been put in place in Oleshky, a Ukrainian city held by Russia. It has let aid in and helped the first civilians leave, with the first arrivals in Ukraine on 31 October.
The White House says Russia and Ukraine agreed to stop fighting there for a while and that Melania Trump helped to arrange it. Lorries and buses brought food and medicine.
Those who left were driven through Crimea to a Russian town, flown to Belarus and then crossed into Ukraine, a very long way round since Ukrainian-held land is only a few kilometres away across a river. Between 1,700 and 2,000 people are still in the city. Critics worry people may not be leaving freely, and a former Ukrainian prime minister said the truce will not bring wider peace.
levels.why: It matters for civilians trapped in the war.

levels.headline: Ceasefire in Oleshky lets aid in and some civilians out
levels.body:
A short ceasefire in Oleshky, a Russian-held city in Ukraine, has let aid in and helped the first civilians leave. The first evacuees reached Ukraine on 31 October.
The White House says Russia and Ukraine agreed to stop fighting in the city and that Melania Trump helped to arrange it. The truce is due to end around 1 November. Buses and ambulances brought food and medicine.
Those who left went through Crimea and Russia, flew to Belarus and crossed into Ukraine, a very long journey. About 1,700 to 2,000 people are still there. Critics doubt that everyone leaving is doing so freely, and a former Ukrainian prime minister says the truce will not bring wider peace.
levels.why: It matters for civilians living in a war zone.

levels.headline: A short ceasefire in Oleshky lets people leave
levels.body:
Oleshky is a city in Ukraine that is controlled by Russia. For a long time, people there had little food or medicine. A ceasefire is when two sides stop fighting for a while. One has now been agreed for Oleshky, and it let in help and let some people leave.
The White House said Russia and Ukraine both agreed to it. It is meant to last until about 1 November. The first people to leave reached Ukraine on 31 October.
They had to travel a very long way, through Crimea, Russia and Belarus, because the front line is in the way. Between 1,700 and 2,000 people are still there. Some people worry that it is not clear if everyone leaving wants to.
levels.why: It shows how ordinary people are caught up in the war.

levels.headline: People leave the city of Oleshky during a pause in fighting
levels.body:
Oleshky is a city in Ukraine that is controlled by Russia. People there had very little food and medicine. A ceasefire is a time when two sides agree to stop fighting. One has now been agreed in Oleshky, so help can get in and some people can leave.
The White House says Russia and Ukraine both agreed to it and that Melania Trump helped. It is meant to end around 1 November. The first people to leave got to Ukraine on 31 October.
They had to travel a very long way. They went through Crimea and Russia, then flew to Belarus, before crossing into Ukraine. About 1,700 to 2,000 people are still in the city. Some people worry that not everyone who leaves has chosen to.
levels.why: It matters to families trapped in a war.

levels.headline: A short pause in fighting helps some families leave
levels.body:
In a war, soldiers fight. People who live in the area are in danger. Sometimes both sides agree to stop for a short time so help can arrive. This is a ceasefire.
There was one in a city called Oleshky in Ukraine. Russia controls it. People there had very little food. Buses and ambulances brought food and medicine, and some families were able to leave.
The leaving was not easy. They had to go a very long way round, through other countries, to get to Ukraine. About 1,700 to 2,000 people are still there. Some people worry that not everyone who left wanted to. Many people hope for a longer peace, but one person said this short pause will not bring that.
levels.why: It shows how war affects ordinary families.

levels.headline: A pause in fighting lets help in
levels.body:
In a war, there is lots of fighting. Sometimes both sides stop for a short time. This is called a ceasefire.
There was one in a city called Oleshky. The people there were short of food and medicine. During the pause, buses and ambulances brought food and medicine. Some people also got on buses and left. They had to travel a very long way to get to a safe place.
Many people are still in the city. The pause is short and will end soon. Some people say it will not lead to peace, but they are glad for the families who got help.
levels.why: It helps families who need food and safety.

levels.headline: Fighting stops for a little while so people can get help
levels.body:
Imagine two teams are arguing so loudly in the playground that no one can play. Then a teacher says, stop for a bit, and everyone goes quiet.
Something like this happened in a city called Oleshky, where there is a war. Both sides agreed to stop fighting for a few days. Lorries brought food and medicine for the families there. Some families got on buses to go somewhere safer.
It was a long way, and not everyone has left yet. The pause is short, and people hope for more peace one day.
levels.why: It helps families who are stuck in a dangerous place.

headline: US midterms on 3 November: polls favour Democrats in the House as prices and corruption dominate

terms.meaning: Elections held halfway through a US president's term to choose Congress.
A poll asking which party people would back for Congress.
The smaller chamber of the US Congress, with two members per state.

levels.headline: US midterms on 3 November: polls favour Democrats in the House as prices and corruption dominate
levels.body:
Americans vote in the midterm elections on 3 November 2026, with polling favouring Democrats in the House of Representatives while control of the Senate depends on competitive races in traditionally Republican-leaning states.
A CNBC survey found voters preferring Democratic control of Congress by 52% to 45%, a 7-point edge. Democrats lead the generic ballot by about 6 points, according to FiftyPlusOne. A New York Times/Siena poll put President Trump's approval at 36% against 59% disapproving, and CNBC found his economic approval at 34%.
Corruption was the top concern for 36% of respondents, followed by food costs at 34%. Gas prices are about 40% higher than a year ago because of the Iran war. House Speaker Mike Johnson says the polling is inaccurate. Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. reports spending $300.5 million through 14 October.
levels.why: The result will shape what the president can pass and how markets and policy move.

levels.headline: Democrats lead polls ahead of midterms, with Trump's approval at 36%
levels.body:
US midterm elections take place on 3 November 2026. Polls favour Democrats in the House, but control of the Senate depends on close races in Republican-leaning states.
A CNBC survey shows voters preferring a Democratic Congress 52% to 45%, and Democrats lead the generic ballot by roughly 6 points. The New York Times/Siena poll has President Trump at 36% approval and 59% disapproval, with economic approval at 34% in the CNBC survey.
Voters named corruption (36%) and food costs (34%) as top concerns, and petrol prices are about 40% higher than last year, according to AAA, because of the Iran war. Speaker Mike Johnson says the polling is inaccurate. MAGA Inc. had spent $300.5 million by 14 October.
levels.why: Midterms often act as a verdict on a president's first two years.

levels.headline: Midterm elections: Democrats favoured to win House as Trump's ratings sag
levels.body:
Americans vote on 3 November in midterm elections, which choose members of Congress halfway through a president's term.
Polls favour the Democrats in the House of Representatives. Control of the Senate is less certain because it depends on close races in states that usually vote Republican. A CNBC survey found 52% of voters want Democrats to control Congress and 45% prefer Republicans. President Trump's approval rating is 36% in a New York Times/Siena poll, and only 34% of people approve of his handling of the economy.
Voters say corruption and food costs are their main worries, and petrol is about 40% dearer than a year ago. House Speaker Mike Johnson says the polls are wrong.
levels.why: The outcome will affect what laws the US passes and its policy on the economy.

levels.headline: US midterm elections: Democrats ahead in polls
levels.body:
On 3 November, Americans will vote in the midterm elections, which are held halfway through a president's four-year term. They decide who sits in Congress.
Polls suggest the Democrats will do well in the House of Representatives. The Senate is harder to call. A CNBC survey found 52% of voters want Democrats in charge of Congress, against 45% for Republicans. President Trump's approval is 36% in one poll, and 34% on the economy.
People say their biggest worries are corruption and the cost of food, and petrol is about 40% dearer than a year ago. The Republican Speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, says the polls are not accurate.
levels.why: Results shape what laws can pass in the US.

levels.headline: US midterm elections on 3 November: Democrats lead in polls
levels.body:
Americans vote on 3 November in the midterm elections, held halfway through a president's term to choose members of Congress.
Polls favour the Democrats in the House of Representatives, while the Senate is harder to call. A CNBC survey found 52% of voters want Democrats to control Congress and 45% want Republicans. President Trump's approval is 36% in one poll.
Voters say their main worries are corruption and food costs, and petrol is about 40% dearer than a year ago. The Republican Speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, says the polling is inaccurate.
levels.why: Congress decides which laws and spending plans pass.

levels.headline: US midterms: Democrats lead in the polls
levels.body:
On 3 November, Americans vote in the midterm elections. These happen halfway through a president's four-year term and decide who sits in Congress, the part of government that makes laws.
Polls say the Democrats are more likely to win the House of Representatives. The Senate is harder to guess. In one survey, 52 in every 100 people wanted Democrats to run Congress, and 45 wanted Republicans. President Trump is not very popular right now. Only 36% approve of him in one poll.
People say they are most worried about corruption and food prices. Petrol is also much dearer than last year. The Speaker of the House says the polls are wrong.
levels.why: The result affects which laws get made in the US.

levels.headline: Americans vote soon, and polls favour Democrats
levels.body:
On 3 November, people in the United States will vote in an election called the midterms. It is held halfway through a president's four years. People choose who will sit in Congress, the group that makes the country's laws.
Polls say the Democrats are likely to win the House of Representatives, but the Senate is harder to guess. About 52 in every 100 people said they want the Democrats to control Congress, and 45 said the Republicans. President Trump is not very popular right now.
People are most worried about corruption and the price of food. Petrol also costs about 40% more than last year. One Republican leader says the polls are wrong.
levels.why: The result changes which laws get passed.

levels.headline: Big US election coming, and polls say Democrats are ahead
levels.body:
Soon the people of the United States will vote in a big election. It is called the midterms because it happens in the middle of a president's four years in charge. They are choosing the people who will sit in Congress and make laws.
Polls say that more people want the Democrats than the Republicans. President Trump is not liked by many people at the moment. Only about 36 in every 100 say they approve of him.
People are worried about dishonest behaviour by people in power. They also worry about the cost of food and petrol. A leader from the Republican party says the polls are wrong.
levels.why: It decides who makes the laws in the US.

levels.headline: America votes for people to make laws
levels.body:
On 3 November, people in America will vote. They are picking people who make the laws. These people sit in a place called Congress.
The President is the boss of the country. But he cannot make laws on his own, so Congress matters a lot. Some surveys say more people want one group, the Democrats, to be in charge of Congress than the other, the Republicans. But no one knows for sure until the votes are counted.
Many people said they are worried about food prices and about dishonest people in charge. Fuel also costs a lot more than last year.
levels.why: It decides who makes the rules in America.

levels.headline: A big vote in America
levels.body:
In your class, you might vote for a class helper. In America, grown-ups will vote too. It happens on 3 November, and they pick people who make the laws for the whole country.
Before the vote, people ask lots of grown-ups who they like best. More people said they like one group, called the Democrats, than the other group, the Republicans. But no one knows for sure until the votes are counted.
Grown-ups are worried about the price of food and petrol. These things cost more than last year. They want the people they choose to help with that.
levels.why: It lets people choose who makes the rules.
